A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Translationese-index research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised, added, and removed material.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic classification experiments, human evaluations, metric correlations, and the empirical distribution-shift analysis in Appendix A.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and reports additional language-transfer evaluations, expanded human ratings, and annotation-consistency analyses.

M1.justification: Both versions compute T-index from the log-likelihood difference between language models fine-tuned on high- and low-translationese translations. No change to the proposed architecture, training objective, or inference procedure is documented.

E1.justification: V2 adds English–German and English–French synthetic evaluations using models trained on English–Chinese data (Section 3.4 and Table 2). This substantially extends language coverage beyond v1's English–Chinese experiments; the existing source genres and QE datasets remain.

E2.justification: In Table 3, v2 replaces InternLM2-Reward and Skywork-Reward-Gemma2 with Bradley–Terry RM and DPO-aligned models trained on the same 5k samples as T-index, and adds a human-pointwise reference comparison. The Llama and Qwen judges remain. Bradley–Terry and DPO already appeared in v1's synthetic experiment, but their participation in the human comparison is new.

E3.justification: The pointwise study changes from 50 translations rated by 12 students to 150 translations rated by over 30 students, with more than 10 ratings per text. V2 also evaluates matched-data supervised baselines and compares pointwise-derived preferences with pairwise judgments. The synthetic classification metrics and threshold-selection procedure remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds cross-language transfer tests and replaces v1 Appendix D/Figure 5's BLEU and T-index-difference analysis with human pointwise–pairwise consistency analysis in Figure 2. The training-data ablation additionally examines pointwise correlations. Appendix A's confounding-shift analysis is retained.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 2's regression plot includes a shaded uncertainty band, without a stated confidence level; v2 removes this visualization and reports pointwise correlations without corresponding intervals in Table 3. Three-seed averaging in Table 2 and the existing significance tests and regression statistics remain.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises retained English–Chinese scores, including in-domain T-index accuracy from 98.00 to 95.8 and DPO from 73.50 to 89.2, and adds German/French results. Table 3 changes 5k mixed-domain T-index agreement on unanimous pairs from 89.7% to 84.6%, now tying Qwen. Pointwise correlation changes from 0.568 on 50 translations to 0.418 on 150, so this is not a same-sample performance comparison.

T1.justification: The likelihood-ratio formulation, independence assumption, and Appendix A's mean-log-likelihood and shift definitions are unchanged. The expanded conceptual motivation introduces no new formal result or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the generalization claim from unseen genres and authors to unseen language pairs. The central claims of graded measurement, human alignment, data efficiency, and complementarity to existing QE metrics remain.

C2.justification: V1 interprets paired training data as essential and greater diversity as beneficial; v2 instead emphasizes effectiveness with unpaired data and distinguishes improved pointwise correlation from largely unchanged pairwise agreement. V2 also introduces an explanation of disagreement through translationese occurring in different spans, suggests multilingual pretraining explains language transfer, and explicitly qualifies the new language datasets as less thoroughly validated.

D1.justification: V2 adds the LLM-judge prompt in Table 7 and reports training on one or two A100-80GB GPUs instead of four 3090s. However, v1's explicit batch size of 32, 800 training steps, and learning rate of 1e-6 disappear; v2 directs readers to the existing repository for hyperparameters. The prompt is newly documented, not established as a changed procedure.

R1.justification: V2 adds Church et al. (2025), Kreutzer et al. (2022), and Rafailov et al. (2024), and removes the Cai and Liu references associated with the removed reward baselines. The introduction adds motivation concerning translationese in multilingual LLM training, while the main related-work discussion and relationship to likelihood-ratio research remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem-formulation explanation, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Section 5 gains a dedicated annotation subsection and integrates disagreement discussion previously in an appendix; the conclusion expands into future work. Affiliations, acknowledgements, and appendix organization also change.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains language columns, and Table 3 replaces its parameter column with pointwise correlations and changes comparator rows. The original correlation scatterplot and appendix disagreement plot are removed, a new two-panel annotation plot appears, and Table 7 is added. Table 5 becomes a full-width display, while the unchanged Figure 4 is relocated.

improvement.justification: Expanding pointwise evaluation from 50 to 150 translations, adding matched-data supervised comparisons, and testing annotation consistency make the central validation more informative. The new language tests provide useful preliminary evidence, but lack comparable human validation, and removing explicit training hyperparameters weakens self-contained reproducibility. These tradeoffs support a limited net improvement.
